sourceSemantics.scope: Two ordinary V1 MUXLP escrow/order-management functions, not leveraged routes or V3 self-delegatecall commands.
details: Static deployment-bound ABI/source inventory, not fresh runtime bytecode/storage identity, balances, allowance, liquidity, financial-safety or successful-execution assurance. Exact grants, canonical calldata/value validation, pauses and independent controls remain mandatory.

Arbitrum MUX V1 MUXLP OrderBook proxy is 0xa19fD5aB6C8DCffa2A295F78a5Bb4aC543AAF5e3. Current Sourcify proxyResolution reports 0xaB66dfEf3722Db73930A59147d900544D7B2AE90, differing from old official docs 0xFD92e0b7107488b095cA98E50BE128fee2a35879. Only actual current implementation ABI/source is used; service labels its implementation match/match, not exact_match. Linked LibOrderBook is 0x09a0dbd7667236106322f6254b605d51e36d4b6b and its bound source matches.

placeLiquidityOrder(uint8,uint96,bool) creates escrowed delayed order, not immediate LP mint or withdrawal. assetId is protocol pool asset index, not arbitrary call target. isAdding=true spends raw asset units and buys 18-decimal MUXLP; false escrows raw 18-decimal MUXLP and selects output asset. Inputs transfer atomically from caller; no separate prefund step.

For adds whose pool asset equals configured WETH, exact native ETH value rawAmount is required and wrapped internally; supplying WETH with zero value does not substitute. Other ERC20 adds require zero value and allowance to OrderBook. MUXLP sells require MUXLP allowance and should send zero value; the sell branch does not reject stray ETH and can strand it. rawAmount=0 is only a whitelisted-callback-account mode, not an ordinary zero-amount order.

Only brokers fill orders after mutable liquidityLockPeriod. Current docs say 18 minutes; older tutorial says around 15 minutes. Neither is asserted as current storage. Owner may set lock up to 30 days; cancellation requires order owner and mutable cancelCoolDown. No caller-set min output, price bound or deadline exists for liquidity orders, and no guaranteed fill time/automatic settlement is supplied.

cancelOrder(uint64) cancels caller-owned pending liquidity orders after cooldown, returns escrowed input (native ETH via configured unwrapper for WETH-backed adds; MUXLP for sells). This ABI also cancels owned position/withdrawal/rebalance orders under source-specific authority/expiry checks, and brokers can cancel expired position/withdrawal orders. It does not authorize creating those excluded leveraged workflows.

Filled outputs go to stored order account. Configured pool/oracle/broker prices, base plus dynamic imbalance fees, bid/ask spreads, 18-decimal normalization, flooring and liquid reserves determine result. No fixed fee rate or price is asserted. Pool requires enabled/listed liquidity asset and MLP-price bounds; insufficient reserves and dependency failures can prevent fills. liquidity-order pause gates fill, not placement or owner cancellation in this reviewed OrderBook.

Owner-configured callbackWhitelist causes fixed ILiquidityCallback calls on the order account before/after fill and after cancel, with configured gas limit; before-fill false/revert cancels, after-fill can revert, after-cancel failure is ignored. No arbitrary target or payload is supplied by these admitted parameters. No callbacks, callback administration, broker fills, rebalance, generic multicall, V3 prefunding helper or leveraged router is admitted.

Current official docs continue to describe V1 MUXLP buys/sells alongside V3. May 2026 wind-down forum topic is a community proposal, not an adopted shutdown notice; contributor Jean explicitly says protocol continues in maintenance mode with bugs addressed regularly. This is not a TVL/activity/performance assertion or guarantee of team continuity. No contract KYC gate appears for selected ordinary V1 calls; user jurisdiction eligibility remains independent.
sourceSemantics.underlying: Pool assetId uint8 resolves via configured pool.getAssetAddress. MUXLP official target 0x7CbaF5a14D953fF896E5B3312031515c858737C8. rawAmount buy uses asset decimals; sell uses 18-decimal MUXLP. No arbitrary token address+payload argument.
sourceSemantics.settlement: Escrow at placement; separate onlyBroker fill after lock; liquidity pause gates broker fill. Cancel before fill after cancelCoolDown refunds original input. Placement itself has no whenLiquidityOrderEnabled modifier.
sourceSemantics.fees: Documented deployed Hop2 _getLiquidityFeeRate uses /1e5 base/dynamic rates, rebate if imbalance improves, capped averaged imbalance surcharge otherwise; target=0 uses base. Bid/ask oracle spreads and normalized-floor conversions affect payout; no current numerical rates attested.
sourceSemantics.callAuthority: Ordinary liquidity orders/cancellations use _msgSender/stored account; configured whitelisted callback target fixed to account, no opaque callback bytes admitted. Transparent proxy admin and protocol owner/maintainer/broker powers retained and excluded.

lifecycleEvidence.postText:
Hi Cenk, thanks for drafting this proposal, and sorry for the slow response here. 
 The performance of MUX V3 has indeed been underwhelming, due to a combination of factors including marketing challenges, compliance considerations, changes in the sector landscape, and development bottlenecks. Given the recent shifts in the perps landscape, MUX contributors have not yet found a sufficiently effective strategy to regain market share and onboard more users without significantly increasing costs. We believe the current priority should be to ensure the protocol’s survival while continuing to look for new opportunities. 
 Although trading volume and fees have been underperforming, winding down the protocol may be an overreaction. The full tech stack of the protocol remains solid, and the system continues to run smoothly and securely. The aggregator’s ability to handle large on-chain positions while offering optimal execution costs remains unique in the sector, and the design of V3 still has its advantages. 
 On the product side, contributors have been proactively exploring new directions that could benefit MUX. They are currently working on a new stealth-mode project incubated by MUX. After several months of development, the new product has now launched in beta and is expected to begin marketing and growth efforts in the coming weeks, with a lean budget. Once the project becomes operational, MUX will receive a share of its future profits and valuation, with the goal of benefiting POL and veMUX holders. Meanwhile, MUX itself is currently in maintenance mode, with bugs being addressed regularly and in a timely manner. 
 In terms of survival, although there have not been any official updates, annual operating costs — including current maintenance, and new project development — have been capped at $700K since January 2026. This is still higher than the proposed $420K, but contributors will continue looking for ways to further reduce costs or increase revenue. 
 Looking ahead, since the new project has just launched, we will provide bi-monthly updates on its operations and continue exploring ways to benefit the MUX community once it becomes profitable.
lifecycleEvidence.interpretation: Wind-down topic is community proposal; contributor reply explicitly rejects overreaction, states maintenance with regular bug fixes and continued operation. No adopted sunset notice established. No financial activity metrics are adopted.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
// OpenZeppelin Contracts (last updated v4.9.4) (token/ERC20/extensions/IERC20Permit.sol)

pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

/**
 * @dev Interface of the ERC20 Permit extension allowing approvals to be made via signatures, as defined in
 * https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612[EIP-2612].
 *
 * Adds the {permit} method, which can be used to change an account's ERC20 allowance (see {IERC20-allowance}) by
 * presenting a message signed by the account. By not relying on {IERC20-approve}, the token holder account doesn't
 * need to send a transaction, and thus is not required to hold Ether at all.
 *
 * ==== Security Considerations
 *
 * There are two important considerations concerning the use of `permit`. The first is that a valid permit signature
 * expresses an allowance, and it should not be assumed to convey additional meaning. In particular, it should not be
 * considered as an intention to spend the allowance in any specific way. The second is that because permits have
 * built-in replay protection and can be submitted by anyone, they can be frontrun. A protocol that uses permits should
 * take this into consideration and allow a `permit` call to fail. Combining these two aspects, a pattern that may be
 * generally recommended is:
 *
 * ```solidity
 * function doThingWithPermit(..., uint256 value, uint256 deadline, uint8 v, bytes32 r, bytes32 s) public {
 *     try token.permit(msg.sender, address(this), value, deadline, v, r, s) {} catch {}
 *     doThing(..., value);
 * }
 *
 * function doThing(..., uint256 value) public {
 *     token.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), value);
 *     ...
 * }
 * ```
 *
 * Observe that: 1) `msg.sender` is used as the owner, leaving no ambiguity as to the signer intent, and 2) the use of
 * `try/catch` allows the permit to fail and makes the code tolerant to frontrunning. (See also
 * {SafeERC20-safeTransferFrom}).
 *
 * Additionally, note that smart contract wallets (such as Argent or Safe) are not able to produce permit signatures, so
 * contracts should have entry points that don't rely on permit.
 */
interface IERC20PermitUpgradeable {
    /**
     * @dev Sets `value` as the allowance of `spender` over ``owner``'s tokens,
     * given ``owner``'s signed approval.
     *
     * IMPORTANT: The same issues {IERC20-approve} has related to transaction
     * ordering also apply here.
     *
     * Emits an {Approval} event.
     *
     * Requirements:
     *
     * - `spender` cannot be the zero address.
     * - `deadline` must be a timestamp in the future.
     * - `v`, `r` and `s` must be a valid `secp256k1` signature from `owner`
     * over the EIP712-formatted function arguments.
     * - the signature must use ``owner``'s current nonce (see {nonces}).
     *
     * For more information on the signature format, see the
     * https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612#specification[relevant EIP
     * section].
     *
     * CAUTION: See Security Considerations above.
     */
    function permit(
        address owner,
        address spender,
        uint256 value,
        uint256 deadline,
        uint8 v,
        bytes32 r,
        bytes32 s
    ) external;

    /**
     * @dev Returns the current nonce for `owner`. This value must be
     * included whenever a signature is generated for {permit}.
     *
     * Every successful call to {permit} increases ``owner``'s nonce by one. This
     * prevents a signature from being used multiple times.
     */
    function nonces(address owner) external view returns (uint256);

    /**
     * @dev Returns the domain separator used in the encoding of the signature for {permit}, as defined by {EIP712}.
     */
    // solhint-disable-next-line func-name-mixedcase
    function DOMAIN_SEPARATOR() external view returns (bytes32);
}
